source.title: Language Modeling using LMUs: 10x Better Data Efficiency or Improved Scaling Compared to Transformers
source.authors: Narsimha Chilkuri; Eric Hunsberger; Aaron R. Voelker; G. Malik; C. Eliasmith

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures cross-entropy scaling with model size, but on a different architecture (LMU-based language models) and a much smaller range than the original transformer scaling work.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own LMU scaling fits and comparisons. Transformer and LSTM scaling fits attributed to Kaplan et al. are cited results, not results generated by this study, so they are not recorded as rows. Figure-only comparisons of per-token loss versus sequence index are included as findings outside the listed versions.
record.test_reason: The study fits its own power laws of cross-entropy against non-embedding parameter count for a new architecture: LMU-based language models on OpenWebText2. This is the original measure in a new architectural setting, over a narrow range.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that LMU models, like transformers and LSTMs, show a power law between cross-entropy and model size. They also conclude that at small-to-medium scale the models scale better, needing about 10x fewer tokens to match transformer loss. They say this is not definitive evidence and that the trend still has to be shown over 6 orders of magnitude.
record.recipe_differences: The study tests LMU-based models rather than reproducing the transformer scaling experiments. Its models use OpenWebText2 and cover 55k to 1M non-embedding parameters; it compares against scaling fits from Kaplan et al.

fits_no_version.finding: Against Kaplan et al.'s cited transformer fit, LMU models trained on 13B tokens match transformers' loss at 10x the training. LMU with global attention beats that cited transformer curve.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Architectures with a sequence prior (LMU) shift the loss–parameter power law down, giving about 10x data efficiency at small scale relative to transformers.

fits_no_version.finding: Per-token loss of the LMU without global attention flattens around 100 tokens of context. The global-attention variant keeps improving with context, like the transformer.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Context-position loss curves differ between LMU models with and without global attention.

record.problems: The parameter sweep covers less than two orders of magnitude, and the authors say it is not definitive evidence for superiority or for trends over six orders of magnitude. No uncertainty estimates are stated. Some comparative results are shown in figures without numerical values in the text.

untested.parts: Range of several orders of magnitude: only about 1.3 decades of non-embedding parameters (55k–1M) were tested. Loss as a power law in tokens or compute was not tested. Transformer models were not tested; only LMU architectures were.
Extrapolation from small to much larger runs; the authors say performance at N much larger than 10^6 remains unknown.
Shape at fixed parameter count was not varied systematically; d was set by a fixed rule.
No analysis of how exponents depend on fitting choices or setup.

missing.what: Individual model loss values and the number of model sizes behind each fit, readable only from the Figure 3 plot. No goodness of fit or exponent uncertainty is given.

record.verdict_notes: The abstract says 'over three orders of magnitude', but the reported range is 55k–1M non-embedding parameters (about 1.3 decades), or 2.5M–10M total. The transformer and LSTM curves are cited fits from Kaplan et al., not runs in this study. The reader's limits_scope label was dropped because the narrow range is an untested part of V1, not a qualifying result. Preprint, no uncertainty reported.

versions.untested_parts: Tests cross-entropy scaling with non-embedding parameter count for LMU and LMU-plus-global-attention models. It does not test scaling with training tokens or compute independently, or verify the relation over several orders of magnitude.
No test of whether fits from smaller runs predict much larger runs.
No fixed-compute search for loss-minimizing parameter and token allocations.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Experiments concern text language modeling; other modalities and training regimes are not tested.
The paper does not test dependence of fitted exponents or compute-optimal allocations on setup or fitting choices, or systematic bending away from a power law.

rows.subject: LMU
rows.size_stated: 55k to 1M non-embedding parameters (2.5M to 10M including all parameters)
rows.operation_detail: Measured cross-entropy across a sweep of non-embedding parameter counts and fitted a power law.
rows.measure: Cross-entropy loss versus non-embedding parameter count
rows.note: The paper says the LMU loss exhibits a power-law relationship with N. The tested parameter range is less than two orders of magnitude, short of V1's several-orders scope.
rows.check: State should be observed. Within 55k–1M non-embedding parameters the paper reports a smooth power law (exponent −0.072). The narrow range is an untested part of V1, not a partial effect.

rows.size_stated: 55k to 1M non-embedding parameters (2.5M to 10M including all parameters)
rows.operation_detail: Measured cross-entropy across a sweep of non-embedding parameter counts and fitted a power law for the model with global self-attention.
rows.measure: Cross-entropy loss versus non-embedding parameter count
rows.note: The paper reports a power-law fit. The parameter range is less than two orders of magnitude, short of V1's several-orders scope.
rows.check: State should be observed. Within the tested range the paper reports a power-law fit (exponent −0.069). The narrow range belongs under untested, not partial.

rows.subject: LMU models (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Compared the training-token amounts associated with similar loss scaling for LMUs and transformers.

conditions.value: OpenWebText2 for the study's models; transformer comparison uses Kaplan et al.'s reported scaling

rows.measure: Relative training-token amount for similar scaling
rows.value: LMU models trained on 13 billion tokens have similar scaling
rows.note: This is a reported data-efficiency comparison, not a test that loss follows a power law in tokens.
rows.check: The baseline is Kaplan et al.'s transformer L(N,S) fit evaluated at 10x training steps, a cited fit rather than transformers trained in this study. The comparison is read from Figure 5 with no numbers.

rows.subject: LMU + Attention
rows.operation_detail: Compared loss with transformers trained using ten times more training tokens.

conditions.value: LMU models trained on 13 billion tokens; transformer comparison uses 10x more tokens

rows.measure: Cross-entropy comparison with transformers trained using more tokens
rows.baseline: Transformers trained with 10x more training tokens
rows.value: The paper says LMU models with global attention continue to outperform those transformers by a significant margin.
rows.note: This comparative performance statement does not test whether loss follows a power law in tokens.
rows.check: The baseline is a cited Kaplan et al. fit, not the study's own transformer runs. 'Significant margin' carries no number or test.

rows.subject: LMU

rows.value: The text says LMU per-token loss is better overall than the transformer's but flattens relatively early, around 100 tokens.
rows.note: This concerns loss over context position rather than a claim version's scaling relation.

rows.subject: LMU + Attention
rows.operation_detail: Plotted per-token loss over sequence index (context position).
rows.value: The text says loss continues improving with increasing context, similarly to the transformer.
rows.note: This concerns loss over context position rather than a claim version's scaling relation.

relationships.condition: LMU and LMU + global attention language models, 55k–1M non-embedding parameters, 13B tokens on OWT2
relationships.reason: Both architectures' cross-entropy follows a fitted power law in non-embedding parameters, with exponents −0.072 and −0.069, close to transformers' −0.076 (r1, r2).
relationships.display_finding: Cross-entropy followed parameter power laws with exponents −0.072 for LMU and −0.069 with global attention, close to transformers’ −0.076.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
